doc.title: Melba Liston — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Working with arrangers and writing for Monk
summary: Bands once resisted her writing but came around; she and arrangers like Oliver Nelson and Ernie Wilkins are friends, and she wrote for Monk without changing her approach.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Have you encountered any problems with the bands and the musicians that you have written for in regards to the way you write for the reeds or trumpets?

Yeah. A little bit, but three or four bars in they’d start over again, and everything’s cool. Not recently or in the last 20 years or something, but before then I think there was some kind of animosity until they got into my arrangements, and they’d say “oo” and they’d start it over again.
It’s like teaching an old dog new trick. How was it when you wrote with Oliver Nelson? He’s a hell of an arranger too.
No problems there? He loved your writing too?
No, not with nobody. Arrangers, we all friends. Ernie Wilkins and all of us real close. I write the soul music, more or less, and they write the swing and bop stuff.
Right there for me all the time. What about him? I don’t know nothing about him.
Did you ever play any of his music? Did you ever play with him?
Did he ever play any of your music?
Yeah, I wrote for him, but I didn’t write no different. I just wrote from my soul. I just write what I write. If they like it, they like it. If they don’t . . .
Yeah. They really don’t ask me to do nothing “outside.” It’s always something like a original or one of their tunes, and it’s a great honor – Monk.
